questions.question: Walk through DynamoDB single-table design — why, how, and when it's the wrong tool.
questions.title: DynamoDB Single-Table Design
questions.direct_answer: **Single-table design** puts all entity types into one DynamoDB table by overloading the partition key (`PK`) and sort key (`SK`). Instead of separate `Users`, `Orders`, and `OrderItems` tables, keys like `PK=USER#42, SK=ORDER#100#ITEM#1` encode type and relationship so one `Query` retrieves related data co-located on a partition. Combined with **Global Secondary Indexes (GSIs)** for alternate access patterns — often overloaded across entity types — a single table handles many patterns at single-digit-ms latency. The price: you must enumerate every access pattern up front; adding a new query usually means a new GSI or data remodeling. When access patterns are fluid or relational, reach for Postgres instead.

interviewer_intent.testing: Deep NoSQL modeling skill and understanding of DynamoDB's access-pattern-driven design idiom
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Multi-table-per-entity design, overloading GSIs badly, not planning access patterns, or using DynamoDB for relational data
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show PK/SK schema, adjacency list, GSI overloading, sparse indexes, write sharding for hot partitions, reference Rick Houlihan talks

sections.title: Why Single-Table Design Exists
sections.content:
DynamoDB rewards schemas that co-locate related data on a single partition so a `Query` returns them in one round trip. This is the **opposite of relational normalization** where you model entities separately and join at read time.

Joins don't exist in DynamoDB — you either pre-join (denormalize) at write, or make multiple `GetItem` calls at read. Every query pattern must map to a partition key plus an optional sort-key range. You pay per request, so fewer requests equals lower cost and latency.

**Single-table design** means all entity types share one table; `PK` and `SK` encode type + id + relationship. One `Query` can return a user, their orders, and all line items in one network call — at the cost of having to enumerate every access pattern before you design the keys.

sections.title: Single-Table Layout Example
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph tableMain["DynamoDB Table: AppData"]
        r1["PK=USER#42 | SK=PROFILE (name, email)"]
        r2["PK=USER#42 | SK=ORDER#100 (total, status)"]
        r3["PK=USER#42 | SK=ORDER#100#ITEM#1 (sku, qty)"]
        r4["PK=USER#42 | SK=ORDER#100#ITEM#2 (sku, qty)"]
        r5["PK=USER#42 | SK=ADDRESS#HOME (line1, city)"]
        r6["PK=PRODUCT#SKU-99 | SK=DETAILS (price, stock)"]
    end
    subgraph gsi1["GSI1: OrdersByStatus"]
        g1["GSI1PK=STATUS#SHIPPED | GSI1SK=2026-04-22"]
        g2["GSI1PK=STATUS#PENDING | GSI1SK=2026-04-22"]
    end
    q1["Query PK=USER#42"] --> r1
    q1 --> r2
    q1 --> r3
    q1 --> r4
    q1 --> r5
    q2["Query GSI1PK=STATUS#SHIPPED"] --> g1
```

sections.title: Designing the Schema
sections.content:
**Step 1: Enumerate every access pattern**
- Get user profile by userId
- Get all orders for a user
- Get order + its line items
- Get orders by status (fulfillment dashboard)
- Get orders created in last 24h
- Get product details by SKU

**Step 2: Design PK + SK to support primary patterns**

| Entity | PK | SK |
|---|---|---|
| User profile | `USER#<userId>` | `PROFILE` |
| Order | `USER#<userId>` | `ORDER#<orderId>` |
| Order item | `USER#<userId>` | `ORDER#<orderId>#ITEM#<itemId>` |
| Address | `USER#<userId>` | `ADDRESS#<type>` |
| Product | `PRODUCT#<sku>` | `DETAILS` |

**Step 3: Resolve each access pattern**
- Get user profile → `GetItem(PK=USER#42, SK=PROFILE)`
- Get all orders → `Query(PK=USER#42, SK begins_with 'ORDER#')`
- Get order + items → `Query(PK=USER#42, SK begins_with 'ORDER#100')`
- Everything for user → `Query(PK=USER#42)`

**Step 4: Add GSIs for alternate patterns**
- `GSI1PK = STATUS#<status>`, `GSI1SK = createdAt ISO`
- Only items with these attributes appear — **sparse index** saves cost
- Overload the same GSI across entity types (status, category, city)

**Step 5: Plan for hot partitions**
- Per-partition limits: 3000 RCU / 1000 WCU
- Write sharding — `PK=USER#42#1...USER#42#10` spreads load
- Cache via DAX in front for read hotspots
- Adaptive capacity helps but has hard limits

sections.title: Query Patterns in Code
When It Helps, When It Hurts
sections.content:
**When it helps:**
- Serverless/AWS stack with Lambda + DynamoDB on hot path
- Access patterns are known and bounded
- Very high read/write volume where per-op latency matters
- Cost-sensitive at scale

**When it hurts:**
- Access patterns change frequently — every new query may need a GSI
- Ad-hoc analytical queries required
- Data fundamentally relational with many-to-many relationships
- Team lacks deep DynamoDB experience

**Watch for:**
- Each GSI doubles write cost and is eventually consistent (sub-second lag)
- Scans read every item — never use in hot path
- Item size limit 400KB; store blobs in S3
- Query limit 1MB per call — paginate via `LastEvaluatedKey`
- Migrations are painful — plan streams + Lambda for dual-writes

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **One table holds all entity types** with PK/SK overloaded to encode type + id
- **Adjacency list pattern** co-locates related entities under one partition for single-`Query` retrieval
- **GSIs handle alternate access patterns** — overload + sparse to save cost
- **Access patterns must be enumerated up front** — adding new queries later is painful
- **Hot partition mitigations**: write sharding, DAX cache, adaptive capacity
- **Transactions**: `TransactWriteItems` up to 100 items / 4MB
- **Wrong tool when** access patterns evolve, ad-hoc queries needed, data is relational

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Frame the idea**
- Single-table design puts all entity types in one table by overloading PK and SK
- One `Query` returns co-located related data in one round trip
- Opposite of relational normalization

**Show the design process**
- Enumerate every access pattern first
- Map each pattern to a PK/SK shape
- Use GSIs for alternate access; overload + sparse to save cost
- Plan hot partitions with write sharding and DAX

**Call out the cost**
- Access patterns frozen at design — new queries require GSIs or remodeling
- Each GSI doubles write cost
- Scans are the enemy
- Migrations are painful

**Close with when to avoid**
- Evolving access patterns, ad-hoc queries, relational data, team inexperience → use Postgres
- Hybrid DynamoDB (hot KV) + Postgres (relational) is common

questions.question: Explain the MongoDB bucket pattern for time-series data — when it beats one-document-per-event and how to implement it.
questions.title: MongoDB Bucket Pattern for Time-Series
questions.direct_answer: The **bucket pattern** stores many small time-stamped events grouped into a single parent document (one bucket per entity per time window), instead of one document per event. Each bucket has a `bucketId`, a time range, a `measurements` array, and pre-aggregated summary fields like `count`, `sum`, `min`, `max`. This cuts document count by 10–1000x, shrinks index size dramatically, reduces storage overhead, and accelerates range queries — ideal for **IoT sensors, metrics, logs, and stock ticks**. MongoDB 5.0+ introduced native **time-series collections** that automate bucketing, but the hand-rolled pattern still wins when you need custom grouping (per-user per-hour) or non-time keys.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can identify and apply MongoDB schema patterns beyond naïve one-document-per-event modeling
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Inserting one document per sensor reading, ignoring index/storage blow-up; or picking bucket size without considering the 16MB doc limit
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention MongoDB 5.0+ native time-series collections, show pre-aggregation fields, and explain the 16MB cap driving bucket-size choice

sections.title: Why Bucket Time-Series Data
sections.content:
Naïve time-series modeling inserts **one document per event** — a sensor reading, a metric, a stock tick. At 100 events/sec per device, a 30-day window is 260M documents per device. Index overhead dominates storage; queries over time ranges pull millions of documents.

The **bucket pattern** groups events by a natural window (one hour, one day, one minute) into a single parent document with a `measurements` array. Each bucket also carries **pre-aggregated summary fields** — `count`, `sum`, `min`, `max`, `avg` — so dashboards read the summary without scanning the array.

The result is **10–1000× fewer documents**, dramatically smaller indexes, fewer seeks per range query, and compressed array storage that's roughly 50–70% of the row-per-event size. MongoDB 5.0 added native time-series collections that automate bucketing internally — but the hand-rolled pattern remains useful when you need custom group keys or pre-aggregation shapes.

sections.title: Bucket Pattern Grouping
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph ingest["Incoming Stream"]
        e1["Reading t=10:00:01"]
        e2["Reading t=10:00:02"]
        e3["Reading t=10:59:59"]
    end
    subgraph bucket["Bucket Document (one per sensor-hour)"]
        head["sensorId, bucketStart=10:00, bucketEnd=11:00"]
        arr["measurements: array of readings"]
        agg["count, sum, min, max, avg pre-aggregated"]
    end
    e1 --> arr
    e2 --> arr
    e3 --> arr
    arr --> agg
    query["Dashboard query: last 24h"] --> head
```

sections.title: Hand-Rolled Bucket Schema
MongoDB 5.0+ Native Time-Series Collections
Bucket Size and Limits
sections.content:
**When it helps:**
- 10–1000× fewer documents
- Index shrinks proportionally — huge win for working-set fit
- Range queries scan far fewer documents
- Pre-aggregated fields answer dashboard queries without unpacking

**When it hurts:**
- 16MB document limit — if a bucket could exceed ~10MB, shorten the window
- Arrays grow over time — in-place updates may move the document; reserve capacity if possible
- Late-arriving data (event at 10:05 delivered at 11:30) needs retroactive upsert

**Watch for:**
- Oversized buckets cause `DocumentTooLarge` errors
- Queries that need individual measurements still unwind the array
- Changing granularity later requires rewriting historical data
- Unbounded `$push` without size cap can silently approach 16MB

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Bucket pattern** groups time-ordered events into one document per entity per window
- **Pre-aggregated fields** (count/sum/min/max) on the bucket accelerate dashboards
- **Upsert + `$push` + `$inc`** is the standard append pattern
- **16MB doc limit** dictates bucket window — choose granularity so peak bucket < ~10MB
- **MongoDB 5.0+ native time-series** automates bucketing via `timeseries` collection options
- **Index** on `(metaField, timeField)` answers most range queries
- **TTL** via `expireAfterSeconds` deletes old buckets automatically

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Frame the problem**
- Naïve one-doc-per-event blows up index and storage
- Bucket pattern groups events into one document per entity per window

**Describe the shape**
- `bucketStart`, `bucketEnd`, `measurements` array, pre-aggregated `count/sum/min/max`
- Upsert with `$push` + `$inc` + `$min` + `$max` + `$setOnInsert`
- Index on `(metaField, bucketStart)`

**Mention the 16MB limit**
- Choose bucket granularity so peak bucket stays below ~10MB
- Late-arriving data requires retroactive upsert

**Call out MongoDB 5.0+ time-series**
- `timeseries: { timeField, metaField, granularity }`
- MongoDB auto-buckets, auto-compresses, exposes normal API
- Hand-roll still wins for custom pre-aggregation or non-time group keys

questions.question: Explain the MongoDB subset and computed patterns — when and how do you use them?
questions.title: MongoDB Subset and Computed Patterns
questions.direct_answer: The **subset pattern** keeps a hot slice of a growing array (last 10 reviews, recent 20 comments) in the primary document and moves the tail to a separate collection — so the main document stays small and fast to load. The **computed pattern** stores pre-calculated values (averages, totals, rankings) alongside the raw data so reads never recompute on the fly. Both patterns trade **a bit of write complexity for dramatically cheaper reads**, and both exist because MongoDB's **16MB document cap** plus working-set economics punish unbounded embedding. Use subset when 90% of reads want only the recent slice; use computed when the same aggregation runs thousands of times per read.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you recognize the write-time denormalization idiom that makes read-heavy MongoDB workloads fast
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Embedding unbounded arrays leading to 16MB overflow, or recomputing aggregates on every read
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show both patterns composed together, explain staleness handling with background refresh, and cite real examples (product reviews, leaderboards)

sections.title: Two Patterns, One Idea: Denormalize Smartly
sections.content:
Both patterns address the same pain: a MongoDB document that starts small but grows unbounded — reviews on a product, comments on a post, orders for a customer. Left alone, the document crosses tens of MB and every read pulls everything even though the UI shows only the latest few items.

The **subset pattern** fixes the size problem by embedding only the **hot slice** (last 10 reviews) in the parent document and keeping the full history in a separate collection. 90% of reads are happy with the slice; the 10% that need history pay an extra query.

The **computed pattern** fixes the compute problem by storing **pre-calculated aggregates** — average rating, total orders, leaderboard rank — directly on the document. Writes do the math once; reads never recompute. Together these patterns make read-heavy workloads cheap and keep documents far below the 16MB ceiling.

sections.title: Subset Pattern: Hot Slice + Cold Tail
Computed Pattern: Pre-Aggregate on Write
Subset vs Computed vs Naïve
sections.content:
| Aspect | Naïve Embed | Subset Pattern | Computed Pattern |
|---|---|---|---|
| Main doc size | Unbounded | Bounded (hot slice) | Bounded + aggregates |
| Read cost | High (full array) | Low (hot slice) | Very low (pre-computed) |
| Write cost | Low | Slightly higher (append + trim) | Higher (write + recompute) |
| Staleness risk | None | None | Possible if async refresh |
| Good for | Small, bounded lists | Feeds, recent comments | Dashboards, leaderboards |
| Breaks at | >16MB, hot doc | Multi-collection read for 'see all' | Complex multi-source math |

sections.title: Using the Patterns in Production
sections.content:
**When they help:**
- Read-heavy workloads where the same info is read thousands of times per write
- Documents approaching the 16MB cap
- Dashboards where pre-aggregated stats hide expensive queries
- Leaderboards, product ratings, user profiles

**When they hurt:**
- Write-heavy workloads where recomputing on every write costs more than recomputing on read
- Rapidly churning aggregates (real-time trading) where staleness is unacceptable
- Teams that can't keep two copies of the truth in sync

**Watch for:**
- Forgetting to update the computed field when the source changes
- Subset drift — reviews edited or deleted later require refreshing the embedded slice
- Compound failures: partial writes that update the child but not the aggregate
- Mitigate by wrapping in a transaction or running a nightly reconcile job

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Subset pattern** embeds the hot slice (recent 10) and offloads the tail to another collection
- **Computed pattern** stores pre-aggregated values on the document to skip per-read math
- **$push with $slice and $sort** is the standard append-and-trim idiom
- **$inc** keeps simple counters atomic on each write
- **$merge** writes heavy aggregate results back to source collections
- **16MB doc limit** is the hard wall these patterns keep you away from
- **Staleness window** is acceptable for most aggregates — design the refresh cadence

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Frame both patterns**
- Subset keeps only the hot slice in the main document, tail in a side collection
- Computed stores pre-calculated aggregates so reads never recompute
- Both trade a bit of write complexity for much cheaper reads

**Show the idioms**
- `$push` with `$slice` and `$sort` for subset
- `$inc` for counters; background `$merge` for heavier aggregates
- Index the hot slice fields if you query them

**Call out the trade-offs**
- Write-heavy workloads can flip the math
- Staleness is acceptable for most aggregates; design refresh cadence
- Compound failures — wrap in transaction or run nightly reconcile

**Wrap up**
- Both exist because the 16MB limit plus working-set economics punish unbounded embedding
- Combine them — `products` with `recentReviews` slice plus `ratingAvg` computed field is a canonical shape

questions.question: How do you use the schema versioning pattern to evolve MongoDB documents safely in production?
questions.title: MongoDB Schema Versioning Pattern
questions.direct_answer: The **schema versioning pattern** tags every document with a `schemaVersion` field so your application can handle multiple document shapes simultaneously and migrate lazily. New writes use the current version; readers detect the version and transform older shapes on the fly (or a background job rewrites them). This avoids **big-bang migrations** that lock a live collection and lets you **evolve schemas with zero downtime**. Combined with **JSON Schema validation** (`$jsonSchema`) at the collection level and an **anti-corruption layer** in the app, it gives you SQL-style migration discipline in a schema-flexible store — without the downtime of `ALTER TABLE`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can evolve a production MongoDB schema safely without downtime or data corruption
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Running a big-bang migration on a live collection, or letting schema drift accumulate untagged variants
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Combine schemaVersion with MongoDB `$jsonSchema` validator, lazy migration on read, and Debezium/change-stream-driven backfill

sections.title: Why Schemas Still Matter in MongoDB
sections.content:
MongoDB is schema-flexible, not schema-less.
- Your application has a schema — it just lives in code rather than in `CREATE TABLE`.
- Over years, documents accumulate shape drift: renamed fields, split objects, new required properties.
- Without discipline you end up with a collection where **three schema variants coexist and nobody remembers which is current**.

The **schema versioning pattern** solves this by stamping every document with an explicit `schemaVersion` (integer or semver). Readers dispatch on version to upgrade old shapes on the fly; writers always emit the current version. A background migration job rewrites old documents in place at a pace that doesn't impact production.

Paired with a `$jsonSchema` validator on the collection, this gives you **explicit, enforced contracts** and zero-downtime evolution — the discipline of SQL migrations with NoSQL's flexibility.

sections.title: Tagging Documents with a Version
Lazy Upgrade on Read
Background Backfill and Validation
Why Not Big-Bang Migrations
sections.content:
**When versioning helps:**
- Large collections where a rewrite would lock or saturate the cluster
- Live traffic with strict SLOs
- Multi-service deployments where not every service upgrades at once
- Evolving schemas frequently — monthly or faster

**When versioning hurts:**
- Tiny collection (< 1M docs) where a one-shot update is fine
- Only one consumer and strict schema contracts make versions noise
- Breaking changes that can't be transformed without dropping data

**Watch for:**
- Unversioned legacy docs (`schemaVersion` missing) — treat as v1
- Forgetting the anti-corruption layer in one service → reads crash
- Removing old version handlers too early — keep them until backfill finishes
- `$jsonSchema` running in `strict` mode can block existing legacy writes; start with `moderate`

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`schemaVersion` on every document** enables multiple shapes to coexist safely
- **Lazy upgrade on read** migrates hot documents under live traffic
- **Background backfill** handles cold documents without locking the cluster
- **`$jsonSchema` validator** enforces the current shape for new writes
- **`moderate` validation level** lets legacy docs stay while enforcing new writes
- **Keep old version handlers** until backfill completes — remove in a later release
- **Zero-downtime schema evolution** is achievable with discipline

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**State the problem**
- MongoDB is schema-flexible, not schema-less
- Without discipline, three shapes coexist and nobody knows which is current

**Describe the pattern**
- Tag every document with `schemaVersion`
- Readers dispatch on version through an anti-corruption layer
- New writes always use current version
- Background job backfills old documents at safe throttle

**Show the enforcement**
- `$jsonSchema` validator on the collection
- `moderate` mode during migration, tighten to `strict` after backfill
- `validationAction: "error"` once stable

beats.text: MongoDB is schema-flexible, not schema-less. Your application has a schema — it just lives in code rather than in CREATE TABLE. Over years, documents accumulate shape drift: renamed fields, split objects, new required properties. Without discipline you end up with a collection where three schema variants coexist and nobody remembers which is current. The schema versioning pattern solves this by stamping every document with an explicit schemaVersion (integer or semver). Readers dispatch on version to upgrade old shapes on the fly; writers always emit the current version. A background migration job rewrites old documents in place at a pace that doesn't impact production. Paired with a $jsonSchema validator on the collection, this gives you explicit, enforced contracts and zero-downtime evolution.
